Alexander the Coppersmith
al-ig-ZAN-der thuh KOP-er-smith
proper noun (figure)
Greek Alexandros ("defender of men," from alexō, "to defend," + anēr, "man"); the coppersmith (Greek chalkeus, a worker in copper or bronze/metal) distinguishes him from others named Alexander. An adversary who did Paul much evil (2 Tim 4:14).

See also: Alexander the Coppersmith

📖 Biblical Definition

Alexander the coppersmith was an adversary of the Apostle Paul who did him much harm, named in the closing warnings of Paul's final letter: "Alexander the coppersmith did me much evil: the Lord reward him according to his works: Of whom be thou ware also; for he hath greatly withstood our words" (2 Tim 4:14-15). He stands in this batch of the named brethren as a deliberate foil — for the Spirit of God recorded not only the names of the faithful who refreshed and served the apostle, but also the name of one who opposed and harmed him. The designation "the coppersmith" (a worker in metal) distinguishes him from other men named Alexander in the New Testament (the Alexander of Acts 19:33 at Ephesus; the Alexander delivered to Satan in 1 Tim 1:20, who may or may not be the same man). Paul's words about him are sober and instructive. First, he names the harm plainly: Alexander "did me much evil" and "greatly withstood our words" — opposing not merely Paul personally but the gospel message Paul preached. Second, Paul commits the matter to God's justice rather than taking private vengeance: "the Lord reward him according to his works" — an echo of the Scriptural principle that vengeance belongs to the Lord (Rom 12:19; Deut 32:35), not to the wronged servant. Third, Paul warns Timothy to beware of him, for the danger was ongoing. Alexander thus illustrates several sober truths: that faithful gospel ministry will make real enemies (2 Tim 3:12, "all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution"); that the right response to those who do us evil is to commit the matter to God's justice rather than to repay evil for evil; and that the church must be warned against those who withstand the truth. The dictionary includes Alexander among the named brethren as the necessary shadow side of the picture: the Spirit's record is honest, preserving the names of opponents as well as helpers, that the church might know both whom to honor and whom to beware.

An adversary who did Paul much evil and greatly withstood the gospel (2 Tim 4:14-15); the deliberate foil among the named brethren; illustrates that faithful ministry makes enemies, that vengeance belongs to the Lord, and that the church must beware opponents of the truth.

ALEXANDER THE COPPERSMITH, proper noun. Greek Alexandros ("defender of men") + the coppersmith (a metalworker).

An adversary of Paul, named once: 2 Tim 4:14-15.

"Did me much evil" and "greatly withstood our words" — opposing both the apostle and the gospel he preached.

Paul commits the matter to God's justice: "the Lord reward him according to his works" (not private vengeance).

Distinguished by trade from other men named Alexander (Acts 19:33; possibly 1 Tim 1:20); the foil among the named brethren.

📖 Key Scripture

2 Timothy 4:14-15 — "Alexander the coppersmith did me much evil: the Lord reward him according to his works: Of whom be thou ware also; for he hath greatly withstood our words."

Romans 12:19 — "Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord."

2 Timothy 3:12 — "Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution."

Psalm 28:4 — "Give them according to their deeds, and according to the wickedness of their endeavours: give them after the work of their hands; render to them their desert."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Alexander the coppersmith is corrupted when Paul's committal of the matter to God is read as petty cursing, when the reality that faithful ministry makes enemies is denied, or when the church's duty to beware opponents of the truth is softened into a false tolerance.

expand to see more

Vengeance-misread. Paul's words — "the Lord reward him according to his works" — are sometimes read as a petty, vindictive curse unworthy of an apostle. The opposite is true: Paul is NOT taking private vengeance; he is committing the wrong to the just Judge, in exact accordance with the Scriptural principle, "Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord" (Rom 12:19; Deut 32:35). To hand a wrong over to God's justice is the alternative to personal revenge, not a form of it. The wronged servant of Christ does not repay evil for evil; he entrusts the matter to the God who judges righteously (1 Pet 2:23, as Christ Himself did). Paul's words model the right response to those who do us evil: not retaliation, but committal to God.

Enemies-denied misreading. A sentimental Christianity imagines that faithful, loving gospel ministry will win universal goodwill, and is scandalized when a minister makes real enemies. Scripture is more honest: "all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution" (2 Tim 3:12). Alexander did Paul much evil and greatly withstood the gospel; the apostle warns Timothy to beware of him. Faithful ministry, because it confronts sin and proclaims an exclusive Christ, will provoke opposition, and the church must be warned against those who withstand the truth. The naming of Alexander, among the names of the faithful, is the Spirit's honest reminder that the church has both helpers to honor and adversaries to beware.
